section_summary: This section concerns Japan’s dependence on imported iron materials and its efforts to expand domestic steel and synthetic petroleum production. Most of the pages document 1939 correspondence about Japan’s oil regulation, its proposed control of petroleum distribution, and the effects on foreign oil companies. The final cross-reference notes concern Japanese interest in Mexican oil, refinery equipment, and concessions.

people.name: Joseph C. Grew
people.role: American consul, as described in the letters

people.name: Nathaniel P. Davis
people.role: Chief, Division of Foreign Service Administration

people.name: Eugene H. Dooman
people.role: American chargé d’affaires ad interim in Tokyo

people.name: Maxwell M. Hamilton
people.role: Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs

people.name: James Lee Kauffman
people.role: Tokyo attorney retained by railway defendants

subfiles.title: Conversation with Colonel Hori on credits and oil companies
subfiles.about: Colonel Hori discusses Japanese credit needs and the future of foreign oil companies in China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hori asserts Japan’s ability to pay while seeking credits, promises respect for foreign rights in China while envisaging Japanese control of its oil market, and predicts continuing restrictions on petroleum use in Japan.

subfiles.title: Japan’s iron and steel supply
subfiles.about: The report assesses Japan’s iron ore, scrap iron, pig iron, and steel supplies and expansion plans.
subfiles.summary: The report describes dependence on imported ore and American scrap iron despite growing domestic rolled steel output. It examines a pig iron shortage, industrial concentration, and plans for new furnaces and increased capacity. It concludes that adequate ore and scrap supplies remain central obstacles to steel self-sufficiency.

subfiles.title: File note on British oil supplies conversation
subfiles.about: The note points to a letter enclosing a memorandum about a Japanese ambassador’s conversation with Lord Bearsted.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to file 894.34/238 concerning oil supplies for Japan.

subfiles.title: Request for an authenticated copy of Japan’s Oil Industry Law
subfiles.about: Attorneys seek a certified copy of the 1934 law for use in a federal lawsuit.
subfiles.summary: The attorneys request the law and advice on securing consular authentication under the cited U.S. evidentiary statute.

subfiles.title: Commerce Department referral
subfiles.from: Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce
subfiles.about: Commerce forwards the attorneys’ inquiry to State.
subfiles.summary: Commerce refers the attached letter and says the writer has been notified.

subfiles.title: Request to Commerce for guidance on certification
subfiles.about: The attorneys ask Commerce whom to contact for an authenticated copy of the Japanese oil law.
subfiles.summary: They cite a 1934 consular report and federal authentication requirements, and request guidance on obtaining admissible evidence.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment of Commerce referral
subfiles.about: Davis acknowledges the referred inquiry about an authenticated copy of the law.
subfiles.summary: He notes that the Department’s April 29 reply should already have arrived.

subfiles.title: Instructions for obtaining Japan’s Oil Industry Law
subfiles.about: State explains how to obtain an authenticated Japanese text and sworn English translation.
subfiles.summary: Davis says the existing English text is unofficial and advises contacting the American consul general in Tokyo. He outlines translation, oath, fees, and remittance arrangements, and says the embassy has been informed.

subfiles.title: Instruction to ambassador concerning certified Japanese laws
subfiles.about: State asks the embassy to assist with certification of Japan’s Oil Industry Law.
subfiles.summary: The instruction encloses the attorneys’ request and State’s reply, and asks whether the procedure previously described for certifying Japanese public documents applies to copies of laws.

subfiles.title: Telegram on planned petroleum sales control
subfiles.about: Dooman reports confidential information about a Japanese plan to control petroleum distribution and sales.
subfiles.summary: Standard-Vacuum’s New York office is expected to provide the details.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Tokyo petroleum-control telegram
subfiles.about: The note restates the embassy’s report of a plan for complete petroleum sales control.
subfiles.summary: It says Standard-Vacuum’s New York office will pass along confidential details.

subfiles.title: Telephone conversation with Kersey F. Coe
subfiles.about: Coe discusses the company’s forthcoming report on the Japanese petroleum-control plan.
subfiles.summary: Mackay confirms receipt of the embassy’s brief telegram. Coe says the details are complex, promises a fuller company report, and indicates that State Department assistance is not yet requested.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs file note
subfiles.about: A handwritten note concerns the location or routing of the case file.
subfiles.summary: Records that the file has been sent elsewhere; the remaining handwriting is unclear.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs routing note
subfiles.about: A handwritten note refers to previous papers and action on the case.
subfiles.summary: Brief internal routing note; much of the handwriting is illegible.

subfiles.title: Record of previous papers
subfiles.about: A form tracks the attachment, charging, and indexing of previous papers.
subfiles.summary: Internal record slip with check fields and a prior file reference.

subfiles.title: Certification of Japanese laws
subfiles.from: Eugene H. Dooman, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The embassy explains how a certified Japanese law and sworn translation can be obtained.
subfiles.summary: Dooman says the consul general has not yet heard from the attorneys. Japanese officials can certify legal texts, and an American consul can authenticate their seals and capacities. A Tokyo law firm can secure the copy and prepare a sworn translation.

subfiles.title: Further guidance to Terry, Cavin & Mills
subfiles.about: State relays the embassy’s offer to arrange a certified copy and sworn translation.
subfiles.summary: Davis notes that the consul general has received no inquiry, identifies a Tokyo law firm familiar with certification, and explains that funds may be sent to the embassy.

subfiles.title: Standard-Vacuum request for a later meeting
subfiles.about: Parker plans to discuss renewed threats to the company’s Japanese business after setting its policy.
subfiles.summary: He expects to formulate a position during the week beginning July 17.

subfiles.title: Hamilton’s reply to Parker
subfiles.about: Hamilton acknowledges Parker’s proposal to meet about the company’s Japanese affairs.
subfiles.summary: He says Hornbeck should return from vacation around July 24 and welcomes a meeting.

subfiles.title: Parker’s update on Japanese petroleum regulations
subfiles.about: Parker says foreign companies still do not know their status under the new regulations.
subfiles.summary: The company has authorized its representative to seek clarification and will contact State after hearing from Yokohama.

subfiles.title: Hamilton’s acknowledgment of Parker’s update
subfiles.about: Hamilton acknowledges that the company is not ready to discuss a definite response.
subfiles.summary: He repeats the Department’s willingness to meet when convenient.

subfiles.title: Attorneys’ update on oil-law litigation
subfiles.about: The attorneys report that defendants in the Kansas City suit have retained a Tokyo lawyer.
subfiles.summary: They identify James Lee Kauffman of the firm previously recommended by the embassy and thank Davis for his assistance.

subfiles.title: Synthetic petroleum processes in Japan
subfiles.from: Eugene H. Dooman, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The embassy summarizes a Japanese publication’s claims about coal-based synthetic petroleum.
subfiles.summary: The despatch lists low-temperature carbonization, direct coal liquefaction, tar hydrogenation, and a Fischer-type process, with plants in Japan, Korea, and Manchuria. Dooman cautions that the publication makes extravagant claims; it also admits delays, engineering shortcomings, and costs roughly twice those of imported petroleum.

subfiles.title: Conversation with P. W. Parker on Japanese oil policy
subfiles.about: Parker discusses Japan’s distribution scheme, exchange risk, oil storage, and the treaty termination.
subfiles.summary: Parker thinks Standard-Vacuum can continue operating on a reduced basis, but worries about exchange payments if shipments stop. He describes Japanese commercial and naval oil storage and raises possible pressure on Borneo. Department officials give no forecast about the terminated treaty and offer limited advice about employees’ families.

subfiles.title: Yokohama office report on proposed petroleum sales system
subfiles.about: The company outlines Japan’s proposed joint sales and wholesale system for petroleum products.
subfiles.summary: The telegram describes a joint sales company excluding the two foreign companies and regional wholesalers that would absorb existing distributors. It weighs selling products on consignment, disposing of distribution facilities, preserving brands, and forming Japanese partnerships. The Yokohama office asks for New York’s views, while acknowledging uncertain quotas and continued government control.

subfiles.title: Japanese visitors’ petroleum interests in Mexico
subfiles.about: The note refers to a telegram about Nakano and Tajima surveying prospects in Costa Rica and seeking oil interests.
subfiles.summary: It links Nakano’s refinery plans in Japan to possible crude-oil and Veracruz interests.

subfiles.title: Purchase of Mexican petroleum for Japan
subfiles.about: The note refers to credit established to buy Mexican kerosene and lubricating oil.
subfiles.summary: The oil was to be shipped to Japan or Manchukuo for a Japanese company.

subfiles.title: Nakano’s refinery equipment purchase and Mexican concessions
subfiles.about: The note refers to Nakano Tomonori’s refinery equipment purchase and pursuit of Mexican oil concessions.
subfiles.summary: It reports a $7 million refinery project in Japan and hopes of obtaining Mexican oil and pipeline concessions.
